risks.title: Establishment of military regime leads to increased conflict and spread of violence across Sudan
risks.risk_type: Future impact of a hazard which has already taken place
risks.rationale: After the ousting of President Omar Al Bashir in April 2019, a transitional military government – specifically, the Transitional Military Council (TMC) – was installed. Many TMC members, including the new Vice President, were aligned with the Bashir regime and guilty of committing human rights violations during the conflict in Darfur in the early 2000s, aggravating anger and frustration among the civilians protesting since December 2018. Dialogue between the TMC and the opposition alliance called Forces of Freedom and Change to ensure a transition to a civilian government has not progressed, and protests have met with increasingly violent dispersals. For example, on 3 June 2019, the Rapid Support Forces violently dispersed peaceful sit-ins, killing around 118 people and injuring at least 780. A military government will likely establish itself for the long term, with the backing of international and regional alliances, including China, Egypt, Russia, and Saudi Arabia. That said, the TMC appears fragile because of internal differences in opinion. This increases the likelihood of fragmentation within the security apparatus, with different factions vying for power, further destabilising the country. Following the recent escalation in Khartoum, increased violence and intercommunal fighting between civilians, armed groups, and security forces have been observed countrywide. A military government is unlikely to pursue peace talks with armed groups in either Darfur, South Kordofan, or Blue Nile states based on historical disagreements. With reduced government influence, armed groups in these regions are likely to take advantage of the volatile security situation and reassert their position through increased use of violence.

risks.risk_type: Future impact of a hazard which has already taken place
risks.rationale:
Sudan’s economy is facing continuous shortages of hard currency and decreasing availability of basic commodities such as fuel, flour and medicines leading to rising prices. The economic crisis is likely to worsen due to the government’s continued inability to address the challenges holistically, including enhancing free trade, fighting corruption, and reducing military spending. It is likely that Sudan will not receive needed foreign investment as the country is expected to remain classified as a ‘state sponsor of terror’
Countrywide anti-government demonstrations that began in mid-December 2018 are expected to continue despite a national ban. The government’s violent and repressive response is very likely to trigger further mobilisation of protestors. A regime change is unlikely, however a more authoritarian rule is expected as President Al-Bashir tries to hold onto power.

risks.title: A rising number of Syrian refugees opt for an unsafe return to Syria to avoid a deepening economic crisis in Lebanon and the repercussions of the 2020 Beirut explosion
risks.risk_type: New emerging risk
risks.rationale:
Inflation, rising prices, and the depreciation of the Lebanese lira threaten the livelihoods of Syrian refugees, who struggle to survive on cash assistance (delivered in Lebanese liras) or receive low to no salary from their employers in the informal sector. Because of these factors, as well as Lebanese governmental policies on return, an increasing number of refugees might opt for an unsafe return to Syria.

While the severity of people’s needs has worsened, during 2020, the number of voluntary refugees returning to Syria was only 9,351 – half of the figure registered in 2019. The refugees' decisions to return to Syria were influenced mainly by the security and safety situation, economic growth, public service availability, and personal relationships in their place of origin, while refugees’ poor living conditions in Lebanon were less likely to be an influence. Unless the situation significantly improves in Syria, refugees are unlikely to return.

risks.title: The declaration of a state of emergency escalates protests that may lead to violence and further displacement in the Darfur region
risks.risk_type: Future impact of a hazard which has already taken place
risks.rationale: Peaceful sit-ins have sprung up in towns across Darfur and in other parts of Sudan, which are also protesting the presence of armed militias. On 13 July, Sudan declared a state of emergency in the region of Darfur after violence and unrest in two towns. The Sudanese police broke up a sit-in in the town of Kutum, North Darfur state, on 12 July, after firing live ammunition and tear gas to disperse the protesters, who objected to a government delegation, who was visiting a similar sit-in. The protesters in Fata Borno in Kutum locality demanded disarmament of the militiamen and a ban on motorcycles in the area, expulsion of the new settlers from the displaced peoples’ farms and villages, the restructuring of the police departments in Kutum, and rehabilitation of the civil service institutions and administrative units in the locality. Sudanese activists say armed groups have attacked a protest camp in the Darfur region, killing more than a dozen people. Monday’s attack came a day after security forces violently broke up another sit-in in Kutum. The African Union-United Nations Hybrid Operation in Darfur said it had sent a team to Kutum in North Darfur state following the reported burning of a police station and cars by unidentified protesters. Darfur is one of the poorest regions in Sudan, with around 50,000–150,000 people in need of humanitarian assistance and more than 1.6 million IDPs in the region. A peace agreement with armed groups in Darfur was postponed after attacks in North Darfur at an IDP settlement that left nine people dead and 16 wounded. Clashes between security forces and groups protesting the violence had earlier led to a declaration of a state of emergency in the region. If violence escalates further, it is expected that the number of IDPs and people in need will increase, which risks jeopardising Sudan's democratic transition.

risks.title: COVID-19 and related restrictions worsen the Tunisian socioeconomic crisis, especially in the south, leading to increased migration across the Central Mediterranean route and growing protection needs
risks.risk_type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
risks.rationale:
Tunisians in the south of the country – especially in Tataouine province, where the unemployment rate is 30% – have been protesting since the Government failed to follow through on a 2017 agreement to create more jobs and development in the south. Tunisia is facing a worsening socioeconomic crisis compounded by the impact of COVID-19. In July, Tunisia asked to delay debt repayments to four countries, underscoring the dire condition of Tunisia's public finances. In July, in a meeting between Italian Minister of the Interior Luciana Lamorgese and Tunisian President Kais Saied, Lamorgese raised concerns over the recent spike in the number of Tunisian migrants crossing the Mediterranean Sea to Italy. Tunisian migrants are the biggest single national group reaching Italy by sea. Since the beginning of 2020, nearly 11,200 migrants have landed on Italy’s shores, more than 5,200 having set out from Tunisia and nearly 4,000 of them Tunisian citizens.

In case of unsatisfactory performance from the newly appointed cabinet, especially in terms of economic and employment reforms, the number of Tunisians and third-country nationals leaving from the coasts of Tunisia towards Italy in search of better livelihood conditions might increase, particularly during the summer months when sea and weather conditions are generally more stable. An increase in departures along the Central Mediterranean route exposes migrants, refugees, and asylum seekers to the dangers of death and injury, especially in case of lengthy response times from rescue teams, raising serious protection concerns.

risks.title: Intensifying humanitarian and security crisis in Kenya worsens conditions in refugee camps
risks.risk_type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
risks.rationale:
Kenya’s refugee camps, particularly Dadaab and Kakuma, are facing an increasingly fragile situation owing to severe underfunding, overstretched infrastructure, and surging new arrivals. Cuts in humanitarian aid have already led to reductions in food rations, the closure of essential services, and growing frustration among both refugees and host communities. In 2025, WFP was only able to provide 60% of the minimum food basket by midyear, with responders reporting critical gaps in healthcare, education, and WASH services. The camps, which host more than 600,000 refugees, are still absorbing new displacements from conflict-affected areas of Ethiopia, Somalia, and Sudan. These arrivals further strain already limited resources and contribute to tensions over land, water, and security. Escalating tensions have already led to ethnic clashes, protests, and police interventions within camps including Kakuma and Dadaab. Without urgent interventions, the situation risks spiralling into a protracted crisis marked by localised violence, cross-border insecurity, or forced returns, particularly in light of Kenya's shifting asylum policies and security stance in border regions.
Gaps in healthcare access are increasing the risk of disease outbreaks, particularly as overcrowded living conditions and limited water supplies worsen. Economic hardship and congested settlements are also heightening protection concerns, including gender-based violence. As services and water availability decline, households are expected to relocate within or between camps in search of support, further straining space and social cohesion.
Kenya’s Shirika Plan also continues to face implementation hurdles and growing scepticism among host communities related to resource competition and security. There are concerns that the plan will only benefit those already with resources (business owners and skilled people) rather than the most vulnerable. Given that, the situation may evolve into a sustained protection and humanitarian crisis marked by deteriorating health conditions, rising insecurity, and the potential for forced or premature returns. Refugees may increasingly move outside formal camps in search of livelihoods or better services, often without documentation or assistance. This trend could heighten risks of exploitation, detention, or deportation and further complicate humanitarian coordination and protection efforts. ([TNH 23/05/2025](https://www.thenewhumanitarian.org/news-feature/2025/05/23/dadaab-voices-what-aid-cuts-mean-kenyas-refugees), [AJ 20/07/2025](https://liberties.aljazeera.com/en/refugees-in-kenya-face-deepening-hunger-as-aid-cuts-bite/)

risks.title: A prolonged Syria–Lebanon border conflict results in displacement and increases shelter and livelihood needs
risks.risk_type: New emerging risk
risks.rationale:
The Syria–Lebanon border remains a key smuggling corridor for fuel, drugs (especially Captagon), and weapons, primarily from Syria to Lebanon, often facilitated by networks linked to Hezbollah and Iran-backed militias. After Al Assad’s fall, Syria’s transitional Government’s forces launched an anti-smuggling campaign in early 2025, targeting routes used by Hezbollah-linked clans near Al Qasr village on the Lebanese side of the border. Armed networks, such as the Jaafar clan (of Lebanon), resisted violently, ambushing Syrian patrols and firing anti-tank rockets. These confrontations escalated into clashes in March near Al Qasr.
Without clear coordination between Lebanese and Syrian authorities, both aiming to stop smuggling, efforts to dismantle these networks will likely trigger more cross-border skirmishes, especially in areas where smuggling remains a main source of income and power for local armed groups.
On 16 March 2025, clashes broke out along the Syria–Lebanon border after transitional Government soldiers crossed into Lebanon and were shot by local Lebanese clans. Syria’s transitional Government accused Hezbollah of abducting and executing three of its soldiers, which Hezbollah denied. In response, Syrian troops shelled Lebanese border villages, killing civilians and triggering counterfire from local clans and the Lebanese Army. The two days of fighting killed at least ten people, including a 15-year-old boy, and wounded over 50 in Al Qasr. The two Governments reached a ceasefire on 17 March, ending the clashes.
Areas including Al Qasr have served as hubs for Iranian weapon transfers, protected by clan networks aligned with Hezbollah. Another factor driving tensions between Syria and Lebanon is, in fact, Hezbollah’s presence along Lebanon’s northeast border and its ties to local Shia clans and longstanding smuggling routes from Syria. Syria’s new transitional Government sees these ties as a security threat and has targeted Shia-populated border zones, shelling villages and expelling Lebanese Shia families. Hezbollah has avoided direct clashes with Syria’s transitional Government so far, but tensions have been rising between the two parties and within Lebanon, between Hezbollah and the Lebanese Government. When Lebanese forces seized Hezbollah weapons in April, local supporters of the party and armed groups accused the Lebanese army of betraying them for cooperating with Syria.
If crackdowns on smuggling continue and Hezbollah and drug-smuggling criminal groups see their supply routes further threatened, localised armed confrontations along the border also have the potential to turn into broader fighting. Syrian forces already advanced up to 5–7km into Lebanese territory around Al Qasr in March to dismantle smuggling routes, and further incursions to similarly shallow depths — meaning within the 5–7km border zone — remain possible, though recent diplomatic talks between the Governments of Lebanon and Syria in April and the creation of a joint border committee may reduce the likelihood of a sustained escalation. The committee, established as part of a bilateral border agreement, is a ministerial-level body tasked with coordinating border management, preventing unauthorised crossings, and overseeing dispute resolution in sensitive areas.
Although Syrian forces have imposed military control over the border with Lebanon, challenges such as difficult terrain, Hezbollah’s presence, and some southern clans’ reliance on smuggling continue to threaten lasting border security. These factors may enable smuggling networks to regroup, casting doubt on Syria’s capacity for sustained and effective border monitoring. Hezbollah could respond militarily to any advance of Syrian troops, not only to defend strategic smuggling routes that sustain its operations but also to assert its role as a protector of Lebanese sovereignty and maintain influence in border areas with high Shia presence. That said, considering the conflict between Hezbollah and Israel between October 2023 and November 2024, which significantly weakened Hezbollah’s military capacity, the likelihood of its direct engagement remains between medium to low.
Given its limited capacity and history of constrained responses, including during recent Israeli operations, the Lebanese Army is unlikely to play a decisive role but may be drawn into localised clashes. On the other hand, Syrian Sunni armed groups could exploit the instability to target Lebanese and Syrian Shia communities in border areas, driven by sectarian tensions and perceptions of Hezbollah’s alignment with Al Assad’s rule, further escalating the violence. Although the likelihood of escalating tensions and an advance by the new Syrian army remains moderate, the consequences could include a prolonged border conflict, mass displacement, and rising casualties on both sides. [(ACAPS 22/07/2025)](https://www.acaps.org/fileadmin/Data_Product/Main_media/20250722_ACAPS_Syria-_Risk_analysis__July-December_2025__.pdf))

risks.title: Escalating violence between the Sudan People's Liberation Movement and the Sudan People's Liberation Movement-in-Opposition reignites civil war, driving mass displacement and service collapse
risks.risk_type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
risks.rationale:
The collapse of the 2018 revitalized peace agreement and the disbandment of the unity government have dramatically increased the risk of South Sudan sliding back into full-scale civil conflict. The March 2025 arrest of First Vice President Riek Machar of the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-in-Opposition by President Salva Kiir has reignited ethnically charged fighting between Dinka and Nuer armed forces, with clashes already concentrated in Jonglei and Upper Nile states. Up to 300,000 newly displaced people add to the approximately two million already internally displaced and over ten million – two-thirds of the population – requiring some form of humanitarian assistance, including 7.5 million projected to face food insecurity during the April–July lean season. South Sudan has suffered from chronic violence since independence. The collapse of the peace framework ahead of elections, accompanied by the re-emergence of organised, ethnically mobilised armed groups, represents the risk of a return to full-scale civil war.
Several factors increase the likelihood of deterioration into civil war. The taking and retaking of Akobo signals an escalation beyond the fragmented, subnational violence that characterised the 2018–2024 period, with organised armed groups now contesting territory at a scale not seen since the first civil war. The mobilisation of Nuer armed groups, including the White Army, suggests this is a coordinated insurgency with the capacity to sustain prolonged fighting. Uganda's continued deployment of troops in support of Kiir's Government risks drawing the conflict into a broader regional confrontation, and spillover from Sudan and Ethiopia could further destabilise border areas. Over 1.36 million people have already arrived in South Sudan from Sudan since April 2023, with services in border areas stretched to breaking point; an additional 380,000 arrivals are projected by the end of 2026. The planned December 2026 elections, already twice postponed, will intensify political competition and may become a flashpoint for renewed violence, whether they proceed or are cancelled again. ([ICG 25/03/2026](https://www.crisisgroup.org/cmt/africa/south-sudan/halting-south-sudans-slide-war), [ISS 30/03/2026](https://issafrica.org/iss-today/race-against-time-to-stabilise-south-sudan-as-elections-loom), [OCHA 12/02/2026](https://www.unocha.org/publications/report/south-sudan/south-sudan-humanitarian-needs-and-response-plan-2026-january-2026), [OCHA 16/04/2026](https://www.unocha.org/publications/report/south-sudan/south-sudan-humanitarian-update-1-17-april-2026), [MSF 30/01/2026](https://www.msf.org/south-sudan-government-blocks-opposition-held-areas-humanitarian-access))

Title: Economic collapse drives predatory violence by armed actors on both sides
Description: 
Prolonged economic decline has left both sides severely weakened. Depleted state coffers and irregular pay have driven desertions and eroded morale, leaving government forces overstretched and increasingly reliant on proxy militias. With formal resourcing exhausted, offensives by government forces and militias have become as much about extracting taxes and looting civilian populations as achieving military objectives. Opposition forces face comparable pressures, with communal militias motivated more by the prospect of loot than political strategy. As both sides are compelled to prey on the communities they operate in, this dynamic risks transforming localised clashes into a self-sustaining cycle of violence, in which continued conflict becomes an economic necessity for armed actors, reducing incentives to negotiate and compounding an already acute humanitarian crisis.

Trigger ID: R1037 - T0605
Title: Entanglement with the war in Sudan
Description: 
South Sudan's conflict risks becoming entangled with the war in Sudan. Though Juba has maintained official neutrality, its close links to the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, which control much of Sudan's border with South Sudan, are widely observed. The Sudanese army is suspected of reactivating ties with Nuer opposition forces in a bid to pressure Kiir and disrupt RSF supply lines — a dynamic that, if confirmed, would effectively transform Upper Nile into a proxy theatre of Sudan's war. Compounding this, Uganda's continued military backing of Kiir is not guaranteed; Kampala's willingness to underwrite his survival is uncertain given South Sudan's economic collapse and Uganda's competing regional commitments. A withdrawal of Ugandan support, combined with increasing Sudanese entanglement, could significantly alter the military balance, accelerating conflict escalation and further collapsing humanitarian access

risks.title: Escalation of inter-group conflict between Jama’at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin and Islamic State Sahel Province in western Niger leads to increased violence against civilians and displacement
risks.risk_type: New emerging risk
risks.rationale:
In early April 2026, the Islamic State Sahel Province (ISSP) attacked a Jama’at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM) position in Tillabéri, marking the first reported direct confrontation between the two groups in Niger after years of rivalry concentrated in Mali and Burkina Faso. Tillabéri is already one of the most affected areas in the central Sahel, where violence against civilians, displacement, and weak state presence have created acute protection risks. Tillabéri recorded the highest level of civilian targeting across Mali, Burkina Faso, and Niger in 2025, with over 1,200 of Niger’s 1,939 civilian fatalities occurring there, primarily attributed to ISSP, followed by JNIM and the Nigerien military. 
The risk of escalation is linked to the geographic expansion of JNIM–ISSP competition into western Niger, where both groups are increasingly competing for territorial influence, recruitment networks, road axes, and local economies. Recent attacks on military installations in Tahoua city, including the Base Aérienne 401 and the 42nd battalion headquarters in March 2026, indicate that insecurity is increasingly affecting strategic urban and military locations beyond the main rural border areas of Tillabéri. These developments have already disrupted humanitarian operations, with UNHAS flights temporarily suspended because of insecurity and repercussions on humanitarian access. 
Over the next six months, escalation of JNIM–ISSP clashes in western Niger could mirror patterns seen in Mali and Burkina Faso, where rivalry expansion led to heightened violence against civilians, mass displacement, and further erosion of state control. Armed group competition and pressure on key road axes will likely expand attacks into previously less-affected communes and towns in western Niger, leading to a deterioration in civilian security and access to services. Both groups may intensify targeting of populations perceived to support rivals, particularly rural communities in contested border areas of Tillabéri, as well as displaced and host communities, leaving civilians vulnerable to crossfire, accusations of collaboration, and illegal taxation. Tillabéri’s existing high baseline of civilian harm, combined with weak state presence, protracted displacement, and fragile livelihoods, could amplify the impact of further escalation. New displacement, exacerbated food insecurity, and deepened humanitarian access constraints are likely as groups compete for recruitment and resources in this strategic border zone. ([Reuters 09/04/2026](https://www.reuters.com/world/africa/fighting-between-sahel-based-jihadist-rivals-spills-into-niger-2026-04-09/), [Crisis Group 20/02/2026](https://www.crisisgroup.org/rpt/africa/sahel-west-africa/321-le-jnim-et-le-dilemme-de-lexpansion-au-dela-du-sahel), [RFI 09/03/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260309-niger-des-groupes-terroristes-ont-attaqu%C3%A9-pour-la-premi%C3%A8re-fois-l-importante-ville-de-tahoua))

risks.title: Continued coordinated JNIM–FLA attacks and blockades increase protection risks, displacement, and humanitarian access constraints in Mali
risks.risk_type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
risks.rationale:
Since late April 2026, the unprecedented operational coordination between Jama’at Nasr Al Islam wal Muslimin (JNIM) and the Front de libération de l’Azawad (FLA) has significantly increased pressure on Mali’s security apparatus and exposed vulnerabilities in state control across northern, central, and western regions. Over the next one to three months, three converging escalation dynamics will likely worsen humanitarian conditions significantly across Mali. The assassination of Defence Minister Gen. Sadio Camara on 25 April 2026 created a command vacuum in Mali's security apparatus leadership. As the junta’s chief military strategist and the primary architect of the partnership with Russia’s Africa Corps, his death is likely to severely hamper coordination of counter-offensive operations, make Malian-Russian tactical responses less cohesive, and embolden further advances by armed groups at a critical juncture of territorial contestation.

JNIM and the FLA are both targeting urban supply chains, favouring economic attrition strategies over military objectives. With the FLA explicitly signalling southward expansion following the capture of Kidal region, citing Gao and Tombouctou as its next targets, and JNIM threatening a full blockade of Bamako region along the Senegalese and Ivorian corridors, populations in major urban centres face mounting risks of acute fuel and food shortages. Critically low stocks in the capital mean any sustained suspension of truck traffic could rapidly disrupt electricity, healthcare, and water access for millions already living under severe humanitarian stress. Towns such as Bandiagara and Douentza are already becoming more isolated because of road insecurity and flight suspensions, significantly constraining humanitarian access and the movement of goods and people.

Escalating resource scarcity and growing disillusionment within the military following the Kidal withdrawal increase the likelihood of intra-junta fracture or countercoup in the coming weeks. Political instability at the centre would further constrain the junta's capacity to manage insurgent pressure, negotiate humanitarian access, and sustain basic service delivery, deepening civilian vulnerability across northern, central, and western Mali. ([RFI 12/05/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260512-mali-%C3%A0-bamako-sous-blocus-jihadiste-les-aliments-ne-manquent-pas-les-difficult%C3%A9s-non-plus), [RFI 23/05/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260523-mali-le-jnim-attaque-cinq-villages-pr%C3%A8s-de-bandiagara-faisant-une-vingtaine-de-morts), [FEWS NET 21/05/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/mali/mali-food-security-outlook-update-reduced-food-access-worsening-acute-food-insecurity-north-and-center-april-september-2026), [WFP 19/05/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/mali/wfp-mali-country-brief-may-2026), [RFI 27/04/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260427-attaques-au-mali-apr%C3%A8s-la-mort-du-ministre-de-la-d%C3%A9fense-les-populations-inqui%C3%A8tes-malgr%C3%A9-un-certain-calme), [ACLED 30/04/2026](https://acleddata.com/expert-comment/heni-nsaibia-fall-kidal-turning-point-malis-conflict), [OCHA 08/04/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/mali/mali-bulletin-humanitaire-fevrier-mars-2026), [FEWS NET 14/04/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/mali/mali-key-message-update-persistent-insecurity-hindering-food-security-center-and-north-march-september-2026), [WeWorld 30/04/2026](https://reliefweb.int/attachments/4aae42fc-2e51-487b-bff2-f923a8d1f7ca/Mali%20Flash%20Update%20%231%20-%20April%202026_WeWorld.pdf), [BBC 29/04/2026](https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cy818zdv831o), [Credendo 11/05/2026](https://credendo.com/en/knowledge-hub/mali-coordinated-tuareg-rebel-and-jihadist-assaults-push-regime-brink-collapse))

risks.title: Escalating cross-border insecurity linked to the Sudan conflict increases protection risks and humanitarian needs in eastern Chad
risks.risk_type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
risks.rationale:
Since early 2026, the conflict in Sudan has evolved from a humanitarian crisis affecting Chad into a direct security threat to eastern border areas. Repeated drone strikes, cross-border incursions, and clashes involving fighters aligned with the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) have already caused casualties on Chadian territory, including around Tine and other border regions. These incidents indicate a growing risk that the Sudan conflict could generate sustained military confrontations, proxy violence, or retaliatory attacks inside Chad. This risk is increasingly characterised by the possibility of sustained military confrontation on Chadian territory involving RSF, SAF-aligned groups, and associated proxy forces operating along the Chad–Sudan border.

This risk is driven by a convergence of security, economic, and political factors. The Chad–Sudan border has become a strategic corridor for the movement of fuel, arms, gold, and military supplies supporting groups involved in the Sudan conflict. Competition over these routes has transformed border areas into contested spaces where violence increasingly follows smuggling and supply networks. Recent attacks suggest a shift from incidental spillover to deliberate projection of force into Chadian territory.

The conflict is also aggravating existing vulnerabilities in Chad. Fractures within cross-border Zaghawa community networks, which remain influential within Chad’s security apparatus, have deepened as communities react to violence in Darfur and perceptions of Chad’s involvement in the conflict. Continued violence in Darfur, combined with Chad’s historical role in Sudanese proxy conflicts, increases the risk of elite defections, armed realignments, and renewed cross-border mobilisation. Historical patterns of proxy warfare between Chad and Sudan may also re-emerge, including support to armed groups and militias operating across the border, increasing the likelihood of retaliatory attacks and further regional destabilisation.

Over the next one to three months, further RSF incursions, SAF-backed proxy activity, or competition over border corridors could increase cross-border violence, displacement, protection risks, and humanitarian needs in eastern Chad. Additional attacks or retaliations would likely worsen conditions in provinces already hosting large numbers of refugees and returnees, further straining regional services, humanitarian operations, and community relations. The risk is not limited to humanitarian spillover and increasingly involves the possibility of sustained confrontation on Chadian territory involving RSF, SAF-aligned groups, and associated proxy forces. ([Africa Center for Strategic Studies 09/03/2026](https://africacenter.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/Chad-Risks-Instability.pdf), [ACLED 08/04/2026](https://acleddata.com/update/africa-overview-april-2026), [Global Initiative 06/03/2026](https://globalinitiative.net/analysis/how-border-criminal-economies-are-drawing-chad-further-into-sudans-conflict/), [ISS Africa 03/04/2025](https://issafrica.org/iss-today/urgent-au-action-could-defuse-rising-chad-sudan-tensions), [RFI 13/05/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260513-tchad-de-nouvelles-frappes-enregistr%C3%A9es-%C3%A0-la-fronti%C3%A8re-soudanaise-font-craindre-le-pire), [UNHCR 18/05/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/chad/core-emergency-situation-chad-update-arrivals-sudan-17-may-2026), [UNFPA 15/05/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/chad/unfpa-situation-report-chad-humanitarian-response-1-30-april-2026))

risks.title: Forecast El Niño conditions threaten crop production and worsen food insecurity in Kenya
risks.risk_type: New emerging risk
risks.rationale:
El Niño conditions are forecast to develop by July 2026 and strengthen through the second half of the year. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration estimates a 61% probability of El Niño from May–July, rising to 87–92% between July 2026 and January 2027. The Intergovernmental Authority on Development Climate Prediction and Applications Centre forecasts below-normal June–September (JJAS) rainfall across western and northern Kenya alongside above-normal temperatures nationwide, closely resembling the 2023 El Niño, when below-normal JJAS rainfall affected western Kenya.
The forecast threatens Kenya's principal food-producing areas during a critical stage of the long rains season. Over 70% of the country's annual crop production depends on the long rains, which extend into August–September in the North Rift and western Kenya. These areas had already recorded below-average rainfall in April and early May despite favourable national rainfall totals. Combined with delayed fertiliser deliveries, below-average rainfall and above-average temperatures from June–September are likely to reduce yields of maize, beans, sorghum, and sweet potato, resulting in a below-average October–November harvest.
In northern and eastern pastoral areas, above-average temperatures during the June–September dry season are expected to accelerate the deterioration of rangeland and water resources. Recovery remains fragile after the 2020–2023 drought and the 2023–2024 floods, with depleted herd sizes, persistent livestock disease, and reduced vaccination programmes limiting resilience.
The deteriorating production outlook comes as maize and bean prices remain 6–21% and 8–17% above the five-year average, respectively, driven by depleted household stocks following the poor 2025 short rains, high transport costs, and strong market demand. High household debt further constrains purchasing power. A below-average harvest would tighten domestic food supplies, drive prices higher, and further reduce incomes and food access for farming and pastoral households. ([ICPAC 19/05/2026](https://www.icpac.net/news/drier-than-usual-conditions-with-warmer-than-average-temperatures-expected-in-the-greater-horn-of-africa/), [GEOGLAM Crop Monitor 02/04/2026](https://www.cropmonitor.org/crop-monitor-for-early-warning), [FEWS NET 04/06/2026](https://fews.net/east-africa/kenya/key-message-update/may-2026-0), [FEWS NET 07/05/2026](https://fews.net/east-africa/kenya/food-security-outlook-update/april-2026), [NDMA 14/04/2026](https://ndma.go.ke/drought-situation-brief/), [IPC 21/03/2026](https://www.ipcinfo.org/ipc-country-analysis/details-map/en/c/1159540/), [FEWS NET accessed 08/07/2026](https://fews.net/sites/default/files/2024-07/KE-Seasonal-Calendar-202406.pdf))

risks.title: Forecast below-average Kiremt rains in Ethiopia threaten food production and livelihoods
risks.risk_type: New emerging risk
risks.rationale:
El Niño conditions are forecast to develop by July 2026 and strengthen through the second half of the year. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration puts the probability of El Niño from May–July at around 61%, rising to 87–92% between July 2026 and January 2027. The Intergovernmental Authority on Development Climate Prediction and Applications Centre's May 2026 forecast indicates a high likelihood of below-normal June–September Kiremt rainfall across Ethiopia, with above-normal temperatures. Severe localised deficits are likely in the northeast and central areas, with at least 50% probability of deficits reaching 50% or more.
Kiremt is the primary rainy season for Ethiopia's northern and central cropping areas, governing the Meher harvest – the country's most important crop season, which produces the most teff, maize, sorghum, wheat, and barley across Amhara, Central Ethiopia, Oromia, the Southern regions, and Tigray. Below-average rainfall would cut yields and household food production. In Tigray and Amhara, poor rains may also reduce agricultural labour income during the June–August lean season.
In past El Niño episodes, Meher maize and sorghum production fell across Ethiopia, most sharply in eastern Amhara,  northeastern Oromia, and Tigray; national yields dropped by around 2% below normal, with localised deficits of 10–15%. High fertiliser and fuel prices will likely limit farmers' input use during planting, lowering yield potential even with adequate rainfall, while raising transport costs for inputs and produce.
Staple food prices are already exceptionally high; annual food inflation reached 13.5% in April, up from 11% in March but down from 15.6% in April 2025 – a renewed monthly acceleration after disinflation, not a sustained year-on-year worsening. Drivers include increased fuel costs from Middle East conflict-linked energy disruptions, seasonal lean season food supply tightening, and trade disruptions, which are severely straining poor rural households.
El Niño typically also boosts the October–December rainfall across lowland/riverine eastern East Africa. Forecasts show a very high chance of above-average rainfall across central and eastern Ethiopia, likely driving flooding in flood-prone lowlands. risks.title: El Niño drives drought conditions, increasing food insecurity and heightening humanitarian needs in Madagascar in 2027
risks.risk_type: New emerging risk
risks.rationale: Current models indicate a very high probability for El Niño to develop by July 2026 and persist into early 2027. In Madagascar, El Niño typically drives precipitation and temperature anomalies, with dry conditions in southern parts of the country and heavy rainfall in the north and east. In 2015–2016 and 2023–2024, El Niño caused prolonged drought conditions and crop failure, resulting in increased food insecurity that particularly affected the country's south. Seasonal forecasts anticipate near-average precipitation in July–September and below-average precipitation across most of the country in October–December. The same forecasts indicate a very high probability of above-average temperatures across the entire country in July–December. Drier and hotter-than-average conditions may affect the start of the rainy season, which runs October–April and is essential for producing Madagascar's main staple cereals, such as maize and rice, harvested in April–June. This may lead to below-average yields, with severe consequences for the population's access to food in 2027, widening food consumption gaps and increasing malnutrition rates. Impacts may also extend to other staple crops, such as cassava, beans, and sweet potatoes, as well as to agricultural labour availability, which usually peaks between November–March. Limited rainfall and abnormally high temperatures may also reduce pasture availability, resulting in deteriorating livestock body conditions and increased morbidity and mortality. Dry conditions are also likely to affect access to water for domestic consumption, potentially leading to reliance on unsafe water sources and limiting hygiene and sanitation practices. These combined effects are expected to increase humanitarian needs, strain local coping mechanisms, and heighten dependence on external assistance, particularly among rural households already vulnerable to climate variability. The country shows a high pre-existing vulnerability to climatic shocks, including reliance on rainfed agriculture, limited water and sanitation infrastructure, and low coping capacity. risks.title: El Niño-induced dry conditions in southern and central Mozambique and floods in the northern provinces increase humanitarian needs in 2026 and early 2027
risks.risk_type: New emerging risk
risks.rationale: Climate projections indicate a high likelihood of El Niño conditions developing in July 2026 and persisting into the 2026/2027 rainy season, coinciding with Mozambique's main agricultural period. El Niño will drive contrasting rainfall patterns, with drier conditions in southern and central regions and wetter conditions in the north. The anticipated event is driven by abnormal warming of equatorial Pacific sea surface temperatures, which disrupts global atmospheric circulation and rainfall patterns. El Niño typically brings below-normal rains in southern Mozambique and above-normal rains to the northern provinces, raising the likelihood of flooding and river overflow. Seasonal forecasts for the October–December period anticipate these typical El Niño patterns, indicating a moderate probability of above-average precipitation in the north and below-average precipitation in the south. The entire country is expected to experience above-average temperatures in July–December, which will compound dry conditions in the south and increase the risk of waterborne and vector-borne diseases in flood-exposed areas. Mozambique's high exposure to climate variability and reliance on rainfed agriculture further amplify vulnerability to climatic shocks. From September–October 2026, delayed or below-average precipitation in southern and central areas, combined with abnormally high temperatures, may affect land preparation and planting. If dry conditions continue through early 2027, crop yields and water availability may decrease, leading to a below-average maize, rice, millet, and sorghum harvest. At the same time, northern areas are likely to experience above-average precipitation, which may be beneficial to agriculture but also increases the risk of flooding, infrastructure damage, and displacement. These combined impacts are expected to increase humanitarian needs, particularly in food security, nutrition, WASH, and health. risks.title: RSF expansion in Blue Nile state triggers displacement and protection risks
risks.risk_type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
risks.rationale:
The RSF offensive launched in early 2026 against Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) positions in Baw county opened a new front in Blue Nile state. This has significantly increased the likelihood of conflict spreading to previously unaffected areas to the north, particularly Ed Damazine, the state capital, as well as the strategic corridor leading to the Roseires Dam. By advancing in Blue Nile state, RSF seeks to strengthen its position to recapture and control central Sudan, later opening a route through Sennar state. 
Following heavy territorial losses in 2025, including entire states in central Sudan, RSF has reconstituted its operational capacity through its alliance with Abdelaziz Adam al Hilu's Sudan People's Liberation Movement-North (SPLM-N/Al Hilu). Access to terrain under its control has provided RSF with defensive depth, cross-border supply lines, and logistical continuity. This enables it to sustain multifront operations and power its advance in Blue Nile, positioning the RSF for a prolonged and expanded offensive rather than a short-term tactical push and increasing the likelihood of escalation beyond the current front lines.
External facilitation further compounds these dynamics. SAF has repeatedly accused South Sudan and Ethiopia of enabling this mobilisation, with satellite imagery from February 2026 showing a logistics camp near the Ethiopian border in Benishangul Gumz despite official Ethiopian denial. If sustained, such external support would significantly raise the possibility of a scaled-up offensive by insulating RSF operations from battlefield setbacks ([ACLED 26/01/2026](https://acleddata.com/report/blue-nile-peripheral-front-central-battleground-sudan-conflict ), [MEE 26/01/2026](https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/sudans-rsf-launches-offensive-blue-nile-state), [AJ 19/08/2025](https://www.aljazeera.com/features/longform/2025/8/19/inside-the-nuba-mountains-and-the-alliance-reshaping-sudans-civil-war ), [ACLED 15/04/2025](https://acleddata.com/report/two-years-war-sudan-how-saf-gaining-upper-hand), [ICG 07/04/2025](https://www.crisisgroup.org/stm/africa/sudan/two-years-sudans-war-spreading), [Reuters 10/02/2026](https://www.reuters.com/investigations/ethiopia-builds-secret-camp-train-sudan-rsf-fighters-sources-say-2026-02-10/ ), [ST 25/01/2026](https://sudantribune.com/article/309824))

risks.title: RSF restoration of siege on Al Obeid, North Kordofan drives widescale displacement towards White Nile state
risks.risk_type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
risks.rationale:
Since October 2025, RSF has mobilised troops near Al Obeid's borders, including deploying combat vehicles along the western side. The sustained mobilisation and positioning of these forces indicate preparation for a renewed offensive to reinstate a siege of the city. A previous siege of the city between May 2023 and February 2025 demonstrated RSF's operational ability to isolate Al Obeid for prolonged periods, resulting in a significant deterioration in humanitarian conditions, including severe food insecurity.
RSF has a strong strategic incentive to restore the siege because of Al Obeid's role as a key logistic and commercial hub linking western and southern Sudan to Khartoum and central Sudan. Control of the city would provide RSF with greater leverage over supply routes, trade flows, and access to corridors into SAF-controlled areas, particularly central Sudan. Al Obeid's role as a major crop and livestock market and a gate for Kordofan exports further increases its strategic and economic importance to RSF.
Despite recent SAF advancements and repositioning in North Kordofan, fluid conflict dynamics and continued shifts in areas of control between SAF and RSF increase the likelihood of renewed attempts to siege the city over the next six months. This likelihood is further reinforced by increasing logistical and technical support provided to RSF by the United Arab Emirates (UAE), which may improve the group's operational capacity to sustain offensive and siege tactics. risks.title: Interregional trade restrictions disrupt markets and deepen food insecurity in West Kordofan
risks.risk_type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
risks.rationale: The continuation or expansion of trade bans imposed in late 2025 by Khartoum, Northern, and North Kordofan states on the movement of goods into RSF-controlled areas would likely further restrict supplies to West Kordofan. These restrictions would affect food, fuel, medicines, agricultural inputs, and other essential commodities. West Kordofan is particularly exposed because it is landlocked and has historically depended on supply chains from northern and eastern Sudan, including routes through Khartoum, Red Sea ports, and Egypt. As formal routes become more restricted, markets are likely to rely increasingly on informal supply routes that are longer, more insecure, and more expensive because of checkpoints, unofficial taxation, transport delays, and insecurity. Alternative routes through Al Na'am market near Abyei provide some supply capacity but are limited and vulnerable to shocks, including fires, border tensions, and armed-party interference. If bans persist, supply shortages and price increases are likely to deepen food insecurity and market fragmentation across the state. risks.risk_type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
risks.rationale: The Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) face growing pressure from key external allies, including Egypt, Saudi Arabia, and the US, to distance itself from allied armed groups with political Islam leanings, including the Al Baraa Bin Malik Brigade. This creates a risk of fragmentation within SAF's alliance structure, as attempts to contain, integrate, or undermine these groups could provoke resistance. SAF remains operationally dependent on allied armed groups for manpower, mobilisation, funding channels, and battlefield capacity across multiple fronts, making coercive integration difficult. Tensions have also emerged between SAF and factions linked to JEM, the Joint Forces, and other groups present in civilian and commercial areas in Khartoum. US designation and sanctions linked to the Sudanese Muslim Brotherhood and Al Baraa Bin Malik Brigade add further external pressure on SAF to disengage from these groups. If SAF pursues integration or restrictions while these actors retain military leverage and local positions, tensions could escalate into localised clashes, checkpoint competition, and fragmented territorial control in Khartoum and central Sudan. risks.title: Long-range RSF drones targeting the eastern supply corridor and Port Sudan disrupt trade and aid delivery in Red Sea state
risks.risk_type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
risks.rationale: RSF tactics have increasingly shifted from ground offensives in SAF-controlled areas to long-range drone strikes. The May 2025 strikes on Port Sudan's fuel reservoirs demonstrated RSF's capacity to hit locations far from its main areas of control using long-range kamikaze drones. Port Sudan remains a strategic target because it continues to host key government, technical, and logistical functions, while the Port Sudan-Kassala-Gedaref corridor remains central to Sudan's economy and humanitarian response. Before the conflict, this corridor handled most international trade, and it continues to support imports, fuel supplies, and humanitarian cargo entering SAF-controlled areas. Targeting the corridor would allow RSF to undermine SAF supply chains and disrupt commercial and aid flows without needing to control territory in eastern Sudan. The likelihood of more frequent or damaging attacks would increase if RSF receives sustained external support, expands cross-border supply networks, or gains greater long-range drone capacity. Regional tensions around the Red Sea may further increase the corridor's strategic sensitivity. Disrupting the dam or the associated electricity grid would allow RSF to increase pressure on SAF governance, undermine public confidence, and disrupt services in areas away from front lines. risks.title: El Niño-driven agricultural losses and water shortages in the Philippines increase food security, WASH, and health needs
risks.risk_type: New emerging risk
risks.rationale:
The Philippines faces an increasing risk of El Niño-driven drought, potentially triggering water shortages, agricultural losses, and heat stress in the coming months. El Niño conditions are already present in the tropical Pacific, with sea surface temperature anomalies reaching the +0.5° C threshold in May 2026; most models indicate an over 80% probability of full development, persisting until early 2027 at strong to very strong intensity.
Seasonal forecasts anticipate below-average precipitation across central and southern regions from July–September, extending nationwide from October. The provinces likely to be affected are Abra, Apayao, Benguet, Ifugao, Ilocos Norte, Ilocos Sur, Isabela, Kalinga, La Union, Mountain Province, Nueva Ecija, Nueva Vizcaya, Pangasinan, Quirino, and Tarlac. Temperatures are forecast above seasonal averages nationwide from July–December. This is likely to produce a poor monsoon season (May–October), vital for maize and rice production, affecting both rain-fed and irrigated crops. Main season rice, harvested in December, accounts for 60% of domestic production.
The Philippines has experienced 12 major drought events since 1968. It is estimated that agricultural drought caused approximately 20 million metric tons of crop losses between 1980–2020. Between July 2023 and April 2024, El Niño-related dry conditions affected multiple provinces, causing agricultural losses, water shortages, and livelihood disruptions. The Department of Social Welfare and Development reported thousands of farming households affected by prolonged dry spells, with losses in some provinces reaching hundreds of millions of pesos. This event also drove extreme heat, school disruptions, and mounting pressure on water and food systems – illustrating how El Niño can rapidly become a multisector humanitarian crisis for affected communities.
In the next one to three months, primary concerns include localised rainfall deficits, water stress, and heat-related impacts, particularly in affected agricultural zones. Over the next three to six months, if El Niño strengthens as projected, drought conditions could intensify significantly, leading to reduced crop yields, livestock stress, water shortages, rising food prices, and worsening livelihood pressures. This may increase humanitarian needs in the WASH, food security, and health sectors, particularly in already-vulnerable rural communities. ([PAGASA accessed 17/06/2026](https://www.pagasa.dost.gov.ph/climate/el-nino-la-nina/monitoring), [PIA 05/06/2026](https://pia.gov.ph/news/el-nino-to-emerge-in-june-intensify-into-strong-to-very-strong-condition-by-year-end-pagasa/), [FAO accessed 17/06/2026](https://www.fao.org/in-action/drought-portal/preparedness/vulnerability-and-impact-assessment/national-case-studies/the-philippines-case/en), [WB accessed 17/06/2026](https://climateknowledgeportal.worldbank.org/country/philippines/enso), [GMA 26/04/2026](https://www.gmanetwork.com/news/weather/content/985366/drought-philippines-2026/story/))

El Niño typically suppresses rainfall across the Philippines while also contributing to above-average temperatures. During the monsoon season, it also contributes to irregular rainfall distribution, characterized by intermittent dry spells and uneven precipitation.  Reduced or unheavenly distributed rainfall, combined with high temperatures, increases evapotranspiration, accelerating the depletion of soil moisture, while reduced precipitation affect surface and groundwater reserves. This can significantly reduce water availability for domestic consumption, irrigation, and livestock, particularly in drought-prone and agriculture-dependent provinces. Prolonged heat and moisture stress can also damage crops during critical growth stages, reduce agricultural productivity, and increase heat-related health risks, especially among affected rural households and outdoor workers.

risks.title: Peace talk end and military offensive against armed groups in Colombia escalate conflict and increase civilian casualties and displacement
risks.risk_type: New emerging risk
risks.rationale:
After the elections in June 2026, Abelardo de la Espriella’s win as Colombia's new President signalled a major change in the country's stance towards non-state armed groups (NSAGs) and drug trafficking organisations. The President-elect has since announced an end to peace negotiations and a nationwide military offensive to begin once he takes office on 7 August, including a 90-day security crackdown involving military deployments, aerial operations, and coca eradication measures.
This shift may increase the risk of clashes, civilian casualties, displacement, and confinement, particularly in Pacific Coast departments, including Cauca, Chocó, Nariño, and Valle del Cauca, as well as in Norte de Santander and Putumayo, which were among Colombia’s most conflict-affected areas in 2025.
This risk is compounded by the significant strengthening of NSAGs in recent years. Armed group membership has grown substantially since 2022. Armed groups have simultaneously expanded into new territories, adopted new warfare tactics, including the use of explosive drones, and extended social control against communities, including curfews and checkpoints. Ahead of the anticipated offensive, NSAGs are expected to intensify operations to consolidate territorial control, while retaliatory actions during the crackdown could further increase civilian harm. In response, the elected President has proposed Plan Colombia 2.0, aimed at recovering NSAG-controlled territory, eradicating coca cultivation and illegal mining (the primary financing sources for armed groups), and securing record investment in state armed forces, with the political and financial support of the US Government.
As a result, July, the month preceding the new Government's inauguration, is expected to see an intensification of NSAG violence as armed groups seek to consolidate territorial control and prepare ahead of the anticipated military offensive. Over the first 90-day period (August–October), a marked increase in armed clashes with state forces is expected, a trend that should persist throughout the remainder of 2026. These dynamics will directly affect civilian populations in the departments highlighted, where most rural and Indigenous communities reside.
Planned government reforms, including major cuts to state bureaucracy and measures targeting officials linked to the previous administration, could also increase political tensions and trigger social mobilisation, adding a civil unrest dimension to the risk.
A historic ‘Super El Niño’ event, forecast to intensify through late 2026, is expected to compound these dynamics. Authorities are warning of extreme heat, drought, and water shortages, with national implications for food security. This adds further pressure on communities in the departments covered by this risk, where access to food is already constrained by confinement and mobility restrictions linked to armed group activity. 
([El País 21/06/2026](https://elpais.com/america-colombia/elecciones-presidenciales/2026-06-21/las-propuestas-de-abelardo-de-la-espriella-seguridad-de-mano-dura-reduccion-del-estado-y-libertades-tributarias.html), [FIP 30/01/2026](https://ideaspaz.org/publicaciones/investigaciones-analisis/2026-01/27-000-combatientes-y-record-en-disputas-el-deterioro-de-la-seguridad-marca-el-inicio-de-2026), [Valora Analitik 17/12/2025](https://www.valoraanalitik.com/grupos-armados-en-colombia-aumentaron-casi-70-desde-2022-crecen-homicidios-y-secuestros/), [Defensores de la Patria accessed 06/07/2026](https://defensoresdelapatria.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/PROPUESTAS-DEL-TIGRE.pdf), [AJ 22/06/2026](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/6/22/far-right-de-la-espriella-elected-colombia-president-whats-next), [NPR 21/06/2026](https://www.npr.org/2026/06/21/nx-s1-5865676/delaespriella-colombia-election), [Atlantic Council 22/06/2026](https://www.atlanticcouncil.org/dispatches/experts-react-what-a-president-abelardo-de-la-espriella-means-for-colombia-and-beyond/), [The City Paper 21/05/2026](https://thecitypaperbogota.com/news/colombia-on-guard-as-super-el-nino-threatens-record-heat-drought-and-food-security/))

risks.title: Permanent military exclusion zone east of the Yellow Line before the Israeli elections increases displacement and humanitarian access constraints
risks.risk_type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
risks.rationale:
There is a high probability that Israeli forces will formally declare and physically enclose a permanent military exclusion zone east of the Yellow Line in the period leading up to Israel's October 2026 parliamentary elections, progressively reducing the territory accessible to civilians and humanitarian responders.
Since the 10 October 2025 ceasefire, Israeli forces have steadily expanded their military footprint beyond the initial demarcation line through tank advances, repeated evacuation orders, the construction of defensive positions, and localised operations. The Israeli-controlled area had expanded from 53% of Gaza Strip at the ceasefire to 64.9% by June 2026, with the trend notably intensifying late into the month. The Armed Conflict Location & Event Data reports that events reflecting Yellow Line expansion and associated military movements increased from an average of fewer than four events per month between October 2025 and mid-June 2026 to 22 events between 18 June and 17 July 2026, a more than fivefold increase.

During the same period, activity by the Shuja’iyya Popular Defense Forces led by Rami Hilles, an anti-Hamas Palestinian armed group operating with Israeli support, also increased. Between 30 June and 9 July, the group carried out three recorded incidents targeting IDP camps in Gaza city's At Tuffah and Shuja’iyya neighbourhoods, including reported abductions and raids, indicating increasingly complex security dynamics around the expanding Yellow Line.

The period preceding Israel's October 2026 elections has a high probability of reinforcing this trajectory rather than prompting a fundamental shift in military strategy. With far-right coalition partners Otzma Yehudit and Religious Zionism continuing to advocate expanding Israeli control over Gaza and negotiations on a durable ceasefire and post-conflict governance remaining stalled, the Likud-led caretaker government, in place since the Knesset dissolved on 17 July 2026, will very probably prioritise maintaining operational momentum in Gaza while avoiding the political and military risks associated with a large-scale offensive.

Territorial expansion is expected to continue through a combination of military and engineering measures that progressively transform temporary military positions into more permanent areas of control. Israeli forces are likely to continue advancing the Yellow Line through localised incursions supported by repeated evacuation orders, the demolition of buildings and agricultural land, and the construction of additional military infrastructure, including outposts, surveillance positions, access roads, trenches, and earthen barriers. Recent satellite imagery indicates that Israel has already constructed more than 23km of earth berms and trenches along parts of the Yellow Line, creating a fortified corridor that extends across central Gaza and, in some locations, beyond the original ceasefire demarcation. These measures are likely to be accompanied by the continued expansion of military exclusion zones and restrictions on civilian movement, allowing Israeli forces to consolidate control without undertaking a single large-scale offensive. risks.title: Continued attacks between Pakistan and Afghanistan increase protection risks, food security needs, and access constraints in Afghanistan’s border provinces
risks.risk_type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
risks.rationale:
Humanitarian needs, particularly related to protection, food security, and access, are increasing and are at high risk of deteriorating further along the Durand Line between Afghanistan and Pakistan given the conflict escalation and air strikes between the two countries. Hostilities have spiked since 28 June 2026 along Aghanistan’s border provinces, including Kunar, Paktia, and Paktika, when a Pakistani attack killed 28 civilians and wounded 49. Pakistani authorities stated that the strikes targeted the Tehrik-e Taliban Pakistan (TTP), which they held responsible for a deadly militant attack in Karachi that killed three security personnel. Pakistan has consistently accused Afghanistan of harbouring armed groups responsible for attacks on Pakistani security forces and civilians, including the TTP, which Islamabad accuses of operating from Afghan soil. Afghanistan has denied these allegations and threatened retaliation against Pakistan for the air strikes.
The latest attack comes as part of a series of tit-for-tat attacks between Afghanistan and Pakistan that started in February. After launching Operation Ghazab lil Haq on 21 February, Pakistani authorities declared open war against Afghanistan's Interim Taliban Authority. Despite a two-week ceasefire beginning on 8 April negotiated by China, these attacks have continued, forming a pattern of ‘coercive diplomacy’ between the two countries. This coercive diplomacy has seen fighting continue until it becomes less productive for either side, at which point they briefly return to negotiations until a new security incident restarts the cycle. This pattern is expected to persist in waves over the next three to six months rather than resolve into a stable ceasefire.
The current tension heightens protection risks for civilians in border-adjacent Afghan provinces (Khost, Kunar, Nangarhar, Nuristan, Paktia, and Paktika), including casualties and injuries from cross-border air strikes and ground attacks, as well as exposure to explosive remnants of war and unexploded ordnance in areas affected by shelling.
Displacement towards other regions of Afghanistan is expected to persist over the next three to six months. The closure of and restricted movement at the Torkham, Chaman, and other crossings along the Durand Line, whether from active conflict or checkpoint closures, could trap civilians in insecure areas or block access to services on the other side. Host communities already sheltering IDPs and returnees face added strain, raising the risk of tension and disputes over limited resources and services.
The closure of border crossings has also halted transit flows and delayed humanitarian and commercial supplies. Afghanistan is highly dependent on food imports, as domestic production cannot meet national demand. This dependence, combined with the depletion of harvest stocks in September and declining agricultural labour opportunities from the seasonal downturn in October, is likely to worsen food insecurity. As a result, market dependence is expected to increase, reducing household income and heightening the risk of food consumption gaps. risks.title: Renewed cross-border strikes collapse the 2022 Houthi–Saudi truce, driving new displacement, disrupting imports, and reducing humanitarian access across Yemen
risks.risk_type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
risks.rationale:
On 13 July 2026, the Iran-backed de-facto authority (DFA) in the north of Yemen (also known as the Houthis) announced the end of a de facto period of de-escalation with Saudi Arabia and the Saudi-backed Internationally Recognized Government (IRG) of Yemen, increasing the risk of renewed cross-border and intra-Yemeni hostilities following a series of retaliatory actions. On the same day, the IRG said it had struck Sana'a International Airport to prevent an Iranian aircraft from landing, while the DFA accused Saudi Arabia of carrying out the attack. The DFA subsequently retaliated by launching missile and drone attacks against Abha International Airport, marking the first attack on Saudi territory since the 2022 truce. On 20 July, the DFA announced a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia, describing it as a response to Saudi restrictions on DFA-controlled airports and seaports. The DFA has already targeted several vessels, including two Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea, in an attempt to enforce the blockade.
Fighting has also intensified between the DFA and the IRG along front lines in Al Hodeidah, Al Jawf, Ma’rib, and Ta’iz, predating but compounded by the deterioration in Saudi–Houthi relations. Saudi Arabia is the main IRG backer, and the deterioration in Saudi–Houthi relations has already prompted expanded military involvement. From 24–25 July, the Saudi-led coalition conducted strikes in Al Hodeidah, while the IRG air force struck DFA missile and drone launch sites and weapons facilities in Ma'rib and Al Jawf. These developments indicate that the escalation has expanded beyond isolated cross-border retaliation, increasing the risk of sustained intra-Yemeni conflict.
The first cross-border attack on Saudi Arabia since the truce is significant because it signals that both parties are becoming increasingly willing to use direct military force to pursue their objectives, weakening one of the key restraints that has sustained the de facto ceasefire. Both Saudi Arabia and the DFA have incentives to avoid a renewed large-scale conflict. Saudi Arabia seeks to protect its economic interests and avoid another costly war, while the DFA is unlikely to escalate unless it perceives increased Saudi military involvement or an opportunity to improve its strategic position. A miscalculation could trigger the renewal of conflict. Further attacks on Saudi territory or attempts to enforce a blockade of the Bab Al Mandab Strait would increase the likelihood of expanded or sustained Saudi and international military involvement in the Red Sea and Yemen. Saudi Arabia has already announced plans for a multinational maritime defence coalition on 30 July 2026.
Escalations between the DFA and Saudi Arabia would likely intensify fighting between the DFA and the Saudi-backed IRG, further restricting humanitarian access. Saudi air strikes on seaports and airports would disrupt commercial and humanitarian imports, triggering new displacement. Supply chain disruptions would increase commodity prices and erode purchasing power. Any disruption to shipping through the Bab Al Mandab Strait would also have cascading impacts on regional and global supply chains while aggravating needs in a country where over 22 million people require humanitarian assistance and 18.3 million are acutely food-insecure. ([OCHA 29/03/2026](https://yemen.un.org/en/312711-ocha-yemen-yemen-humanitarian-needs-and-response-plan-2026-march-2026), [JP 25/07/2026](https://www.jpost.com/middle-east/article-903606), [Reuters 24/07/2026](https://www.reuters.com/world/middle-east/yemen-teeters-towards-renewed-war-shadow-iran-conflict-2026-07-24/), [ICG 17/07/2026](https://www.crisisgroup.org/qna/middle-east-north-africa/yemen-iran-saudi-arabia/yemens-de-facto-truce-risk-how-prevent-return-war), [AJ 05/07/2026](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/7/5/at-least-15-yemeni-government-troops-killed-in-hodeidah-fighting), [The Guardian 23/07/2026](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/jul/23/houthis-claim-attack-ship-tanker-saudi-arabia-red-sea), [Reuters 23/07/2026](https://www.reuters.com/world/middle-east/houthis-say-they-attacked-saudi-tankers-red-sea-threatening-new-chokepoint-iran-2026-07-23/), [Arab News 25/07/2026](https://www.arabnews.com/node/2652234/middle-east), [SPA 25/07/2026](https://www.spa.gov.sa/en/N2640956))

risks.title: Escalating insecurity across the Lake Chad Basin increases displacement, protection risks, and humanitarian access constraints
risks.risk_type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
risks.rationale:
Violence involving Boko Haram and Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP) is rising after five years of declining lethality in the Lake Chad Basin. More than 300 clashes involving the two groups were recorded in the first quarter of 2026, 30% above the previous quarter, while militant Islamist-linked fatalities increased by 28% over the past year, reaching their highest level since 2015. Nigeria accounted for 87% of these fatalities, with Borno remaining the expected epicentre, followed by affected areas of Adamawa and Yobe.
The escalation is expected to be driven by two related developments. While regional forces have concentrated military operations against ISWAP, Boko Haram has regrouped and rebuilt its capacity to launch coordinated attacks against military bases. At the same time, the May killing of senior ISWAP leader Abu-Bilal Al Minuki is expected to trigger retaliatory attacks and greater competition between factions for territorial influence and legitimacy. ISWAP has overrun at least 16 Nigerian military bases over the past year, while its increasing use of improvised explosive devices and reconnaissance drones enhances its capacity to identify, isolate, and attack military positions, increasing the operational threat posed by the group.
Over the next three to six months, there is a very high probability that intensified insurgent attacks and military counteroperations will increase civilian casualties, displacement, and humanitarian access constraints across the basin. Violence is expected to remain concentrated in Borno, with continued spillover into Adamawa and Yobe, where Boko Haram and ISWAP are likely to intensify attacks on civilians, military positions, and transport routes. Escalating violence in northeastern Nigeria is expected to generate additional refugee movements into Niger's Diffa region, while military pressure and cross-border armed group movements may contribute to increased attacks, abductions, and disruptions to fishing and trade in Cameroon’s Far North, as well as renewed displacement and protection risks in Chad’s Lac province. These cross-border displacement dynamics and parallel insecurity are expected to reverse recent stabilisation gains and generate additional humanitarian needs across the Lake Chad Basin. ([ICG 09/07/2026](https://www.crisisgroup.org/oth/chad-cuba-horn-africa-pakistan/horizon-july-december-2026), [OCHA 07/07/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/nigeria/lake-chad-basin-humanitarian-overview-2026-29-june-2026), [OCHA 29/04/2026](https://www.unocha.org/publications/report/nigeria/lake-chad-basin-humanitarian-overview-29-april-2026), [RFI 23/06/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260623-aux-confins-nord-du-cameroun-une-commune-enclav%C3%A9e-sous-une-pression-jihadiste-constante), [AJ 18/05/2026](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/5/18/how-iswap-and-boko-haram-are-reshaping-the-lake-chad-basin), [UNHCR 02/07/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/cameroon/lake-chad-basin-regional-protection-and-displacement-crisis-humanitarian-priorities-and-funding-needs-across-cameroon-chad-niger-and-nigeria-june-december-2026), [UNHCR 03/07/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/cameroon/unhcr-warns-lake-chad-basin-tipping-point-violence-and-displacement-surge), [ACLED 19/05/2026](https://acleddata.com/expert-comment/violence-involving-boko-haram-and-islamic-state-west-africa-province-rising), [ACSS 06/04/2026](https://africacenter.org/spotlight/2026a-mig-widening-militant-islamist-threat/))

risks.title: Escalating clashes between Interim Taliban Authority forces and armed opposition groups in Badakhshan deteriorates food security and increases protection risks
risks.risk_type: New emerging risk
risks.rationale:
Persistent tension in Badakhshan, driven by disputes over mining resources, ethnic differences, contested territorial control, and grievances over Interim Taliban Authority (ITA) governance, risk creating recurrent instability and protection risks for communities.
Armed opposition to the ITA has been building in the province over the course of 2026. ACLED recorded 22 anti-ITA armed-opposition events in Badakhshan between January–July 2026, up from just four between June–December 2025. While the recent surrender of Fateh-aligned fighters has eased the immediate risk of renewed clashes, the ITA's broader efforts to consolidate control over powerful opposition commanders and curb their influence are likely to generate resentment among these groups, increasing the risk of further infighting.
ACLED forecasts at least 34 violent events nationwide in September 2026, of which 19 (roughly 56%) are projected to occur in Badakhshan alone, meaning a 17% rise in violence against civilians compared to the previous month's average. This indicates Badakhshan province is becoming a potential point for national conflict risk.
The province has valuable mineral deposits, including gold and lapis lazuli, and has long been contested. Recent clashes were triggered by the ITA suspension of gold mining activities in parts of the province to disarm fighters of opposition groups.
Clashes have occurred across multiple districts in 2026, including a brief seizure of the Yaftal-e Sufla district headquarters and Afghanistan Freedom Front clashes with ITA forces in Zebak in July. Repeated fighting over district centres risks triggering intermittent displacement as families flee active front lines and may expose residents to crossfire, checkpoint violence, and casualties. Badakhshan’s current context indicates a risk of rising displacement and protection needs, reduced humanitarian access to respond to them, and a deteriorating food security outlook.
